how-much-to-charge-to-pump-a-septic-tank.text:
← Septic pumping bid calculator

How much to charge to pump a septic tank

The number a homeowner wants is a published “$325 pump special.” That number is not a takeoff. A 1,000-gallon tank with an exposed lid and the truck at the riser is not the same job as a 1,500-gallon two-tank system with a buried lid, a 150-foot hose, baffles, and an inspection. The word “pump” is the same. The hours are not.

Open the free bid calculator

Count the lid and the extra gallons, not just the special

Basement-waterproofing calculators price wells, a pit, and discharge. Water-heater calculators price a vent, a gas upsize, and an attic. Junk-removal calculators price haul volume and a landfill ticket. A septic stop is a service: the included gallons, the access to the lid, the hose the truck cannot get closer on, extra tanks, and the dump fee. Quoting all of that from a published special is how the first buried lid eats the field margin.

A job with a similar primary tank can cost much more

Each buried lid is locate-and-dig that never appears on the brochure. Extra gallons over the included pump are billed as their own hours and their own dump ticket. A second tank, baffles, risers, and a written inspection are adders that get forgotten on a driveway special. On the sample rates a two-tank buried job with 2,000 gallons, a 150-foot hose, baffles, two risers, and an inspection prices about $1,972 ($0.99 per gallon pumped, 9.4 crew-hours). The same shop’s 1,000-gallon exposed-lid driveway pump prices about $488 ($0.49 per gallon, 1.8 hours, walk-away $351). Matching the brochure job’s per-gallon number — or a $325 special — on the two-tank stop is how that job becomes a loss.

An after-hours emergency is not automatically the expensive one

A 1,500-gallon buried emergency with one extra tank and a 120-foot hose is not the two-tank inspection job plus 50%. On the sample rates that after-hours stop prices about $1,311 ($0.66 per gallon, 6.5 crew-hours) — more than the brochure special, less than the two-tank buried takeoff, because the risers, baffles, and written report do not live in a published emergency adder. A typical 1,250-gallon buried lid with one riser and 80 feet of hose prices about $1,002 (4.3 hours). Treating either as a blended add-on is how the special that looked fine turns into a loss after the first dig.

Load the wage, then keep a walk-away number

A $38/h pumper loaded at 32% payroll burden is $50.16. Margin is a share of the price you send, not a markup on cost. The walk-away price is total cost — below that the job makes nothing before you take a dollar home. On the sample rates even the brochure driveway pump walks away at $351, which is why a $325 special is already a loss before the first extra hose foot. Replace every rate with your dump tickets before you send either number.

What this is not

This is not a septic design, a building-code determination, a permit, an environmental report, or a recommended market price. It is arithmetic on the numbers you type. Tank size, access, hose run, extra tanks, and whether the stop is after-hours are yours to confirm.

Price your next pump

Common questions

How much to charge to pump a septic tank?

Charge from the included gallons, extra gallons over that include, buried-lid locate-and-dig, hose beyond the included run, extra tanks, baffles, risers, inspection, after-hours dispatch, dump tickets, loaded labor, overhead, and a margin that is a share of price. A default 1,000-gallon exposed-lid driveway pump at the sample rates in this calculator prices around $488 — about $0.49 per gallon.

Why is a flat pump-special quote dangerous?

Homeowners count 'a pump is a pump.' Extra gallons, a buried lid, a long hose, a second tank, baffles, risers, and emergency dispatch do not live in a $325 special. Matching a cheaper per-gallon quote written for a brochure driveway stop is how a two-tank buried job becomes a loss.

Does a larger tank always cost more to pump?

Not in proportion. On the sample rates a two-tank buried job with 2,000 gallons, a 150-foot hose, baffles, two risers, and an inspection prices around $1,972 ($0.99 per gallon), while a 1,000-gallon exposed-lid driveway pump prices around $488 ($0.49 per gallon).

      Hand the customer a proposal

      Common questions

      Why is disposal the biggest single cost on the job?

      Because the treatment plant charges by volume and does not care how easy the pump-out was. On the defaults, disposal of 1,000 gallons is $160 against $87.78 of loaded labor for 1.75 hours. That is the line most likely to change without warning when a receiving facility reprices, and the one worth re-checking before you honour an old quote.

      Can I reuse the $0.49 per gallon figure as a rate?

      No, and it is shown as a check rather than a rate for that reason. It is simply $487.81 divided by 1,000 gallons, and it falls as volume rises because the trip, the site time, and the travel charge are fixed. A 1,500-gallon tank does not cost 50% more. Quote from the tank size and the access conditions, then use the per-gallon number only to compare against what a competitor advertised.

      Why is hose footage free at 40 feet?

      Because the truck carries 50 ft in the base price. Only footage past that allowance bills, and the defaults sit 10 ft inside it. Long hose pulls are worth entering accurately: they are hard physical work, they slow the job, and they are the usual reason a tank that looked routine from the driveway is not.

      What is not included on the defaults?

      Uncovering a buried lid, baffle replacement, risers, a written inspection report, and the $125 after-hours premium are all off. The $45 permit is entered but not applied unless your jurisdiction requires one for a routine pump-out. These are the extras that turn a $488 service call into a several-hour job, so switch on the ones the site actually needs before quoting.

vs-a-flat-pump-special.html.text:
← Septic Pumping Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat pump special

“$X, any tank, pumped” is not a price for a septic stop — it is a price for an exposed lid and one tank at the included gallons, quietly applied to a buried, two-tank system with baffles and risers too.

What a flat pump special is

A flat pump special is the fastest way to quote a septic stop over the phone: name a number and go. Homeowners like it because it is easy to compare against a competitor's coupon, and it is the number a customer holding one will ask you to match.

The number behind it was usually set for the simplest version of the job — an exposed lid, the truck parked at the tank, one tank at or under the included gallons — and then reused for every call afterward, whether or not the next one has a buried lid, a second tank or pump chamber, baffles, risers, or an inspection report the homeowner asks for once the truck is already there.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter tank gallons, any extra tanks or a pump chamber, hose footage, whether the lid is exposed or buried, baffle replacement, risers, a written inspection report, after-hours dispatch, and your own wage, payroll burden, travel, overhead, and target margin. It prices gallons and hose past the included amount, the buried-lid dig, and every extra as their own lines on top of the base stop, and returns the price, the crew-hour split, the effective hourly rate, and the walk-away price — for this job, not a flat number for every tank.

What a flat pump special doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges the same price whether the lid is sitting exposed at grade or has to be located and dug out of the lawn. Prices a buried lid as its own locate-and-dig hours, separate from the base pump.
Bills the same for a 1,000-gallon single tank and a 2,000-gallon two-tank system, even though the extra gallons and the second tank add hours and dump-fee gallons the special never counted. Prices gallons past the included amount per 100 gallons, and extra tanks or a pump chamber as their own line, on top of the primary tank.
Has no line for baffle replacement, risers, or a written inspection report, which are commonly sold once the truck is already on site. Prices baffles, each riser, and an inspection report as their own hours and material cost.
Has no premium for an after-hours or emergency call, even though that is often the reason the call came in at all. Applies an after-hours dispatch line to hours and fee when the stop is scheduled outside normal hours.
Gives the estimator a number to quote, not a number to check a quote against. Reports the price, the profit, and the effective hourly rate, so a shopped price can be scored against real cost before you commit to it.

The same pump special, two different jobs

Using this calculator's own shipped defaults, at a 28% target margin, a $38 hourly wage, 32% payroll burden, and $55 in travel and equipment:

An exposed-lid, 1,000-gallon single tank with a 40 ft hose — the brochure job — costs $351.22 to run and this calculator prices it at $487.81. The same call, but the lid is buried, the tank is 1,250 gallons with a 750-gallon second tank (2,000 gallons total), the hose run is 150 ft, and the job adds baffle replacement, two risers, and a written inspection report: that job costs $1,419.85 to run — 4.04 times the brochure job's cost, on the same base stop — and this calculator prices it at $1,972.02, still the target 28% margin. Quote the two-tank job at the pump special's flat $487.81 price instead, and it prices $932.04 below its own break-even cost — before counting the $1,484.21 it falls short of this calculator's own price. Same pump special, one job that pays and one that loses money the moment the shovel and the baffle kit show up.

Common questions

Why does a flat pump special get a buried, multi-tank job wrong?

Because the special was priced for an exposed lid and one tank at the included gallons and hose run, and the cost drivers for a buried, multi-tank job are not in that price at all. Using this calculator's own shipped defaults, a 1,000-gallon exposed-lid tank with a 40 ft hose costs $351.22 to run, and a two-tank, 2,000-gallon buried system with baffles, two risers, an inspection report, and a 150 ft hose costs $1,419.85 to run -- 4.04 times as much, on the same base stop.

What does a flat pump special usually leave out entirely?

The dig and the extras. A pump special has no line for locating and digging a buried lid, no line for gallons or hose footage past the included amount, and no line for a second tank, a pump chamber, baffle replacement, risers, or a written inspection report. It also has no line for after-hours or emergency dispatch, which is commonly the reason the call came in at all.

How big is the pricing gap in practice?

On this calculator's own shipped defaults: the exposed-lid, single-tank stop prices at $487.81, on a job that costs $351.22 to run, holding a 28% target margin. The two-tank, buried, baffles-and-risers job costs $1,419.85 to run, and this calculator prices it at $1,972.02, still the same 28% margin. Quoting that job at the pump special's $487.81 price leaves it $932.04 below its own break-even cost -- before counting the $1,484.21 shortfall against what this calculator prices the same job at.

Is a flat pump special ever the right way to quote?

For a narrow band of jobs -- an exposed lid, a single tank at or under the included gallons, hose within the included run, and no extras -- a flat pump special can land close, because that is probably the job the price was set on. The risk is quoting a buried lid, a second tank, baffles, risers, an inspection, or an after-hours call sight unseen, because the special does not know what is under the lawn until someone digs, and by then the flat number has often already been quoted over the phone.

Does this calculator know my local labor rates or disposal fees?

No. It has no data on your local labor market, your dump facility's fees, or what other pumpers in your area charge. It takes tank gallons, extra tanks, hose footage, access type, baffles, risers, an inspection report, after-hours dispatch, and your own wage, burden, travel, overhead, and target margin, and turns that into a price for this job -- the arithmetic a flat pump special skips, not a market survey.

vs-servicecore.html.text:
← Septic Pumping Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. ServiceCore

Two different shapes: ServiceCore routes, dispatches, and invoices a septic fleet across a whole company. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — what should this one pump-out cost, given its gallons, hose pull, access, and disposal, before you quote it.

What each tool is for

ServiceCore is business software built for septic, portable restroom, and dumpster rental operators — a narrower niche than a general field-service platform, and one that covers the pumping side of this trade directly. Its published feature set covers route optimisation and dispatch, scheduling, job and asset management, invoicing and payment collection, compliance record-keeping, and a mobile app that puts the day's schedule, driving directions, job notes, signature capture and photo upload in the driver's hand. It is sold as an ongoing subscription for a company. ServiceCore's own pricing page is not reachable from this session to confirm today's plan names or dollar figures, so none is invented here: only its well-documented identity and category — septic and liquid-waste business management software, sold as a subscription — are stated, and no dollar amount for ServiceCore appears on this page.

This calculator does none of what ServiceCore does. It does not route a truck, dispatch a driver, hold a compliance record, or store a customer on a server. It takes one stop's tank gallons, any extra tanks on the same site, hose pull distance, how hard the lid is to reach, riser count and cost, baffle replacement, disposal cost per gallon, the dump-trip fee, an after-hours premium, loaded wage and payroll burden, overhead, travel, and target margin, and turns that into the per-job price and the walk-away price below which the stop loses money — plus, if you already have a number on the table, a check of whether it clears that floor, and a printable customer proposal for that one job. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.

Most septic operators get different value from each: ServiceCore (or a comparable liquid-waste platform) for routing, dispatching, invoicing and compliance across a whole fleet, and a private calculator like this one for an instant, no-login gut-check on what one stop should cost before a business system is involved. This page's own figures are a pricing model, not a scheduled job, an invoice, or a signed proposal.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off — which matters at a rural tank with no signal.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or ServiceCore?

They do different jobs, and a septic business of any size may end up using both. ServiceCore is business software built for septic and liquid-waste companies: it optimises truck routes, dispatches and schedules jobs, tracks assets, handles invoicing and payment, keeps compliance records, and gives drivers a mobile app carrying the day's schedule, directions, job notes, signature capture and photos. It is sold as an ongoing subscription for a company. This calculator does one narrower thing: starting from tank gallons, any extra tanks on the same site, hose pull distance, how hard the lid is to reach, riser and baffle work, disposal cost per gallon, the dump-trip fee, after-hours premium, loaded wage and payroll burden, overhead, travel, and target margin, it turns that into the per-job price and the walk-away price below which the stop loses money. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type. A septic company already routing trucks, dispatching drivers, and invoicing across a fleet is better served by ServiceCore or a comparable liquid-waste platform; an operator who wants an instant, private gut-check on what one pump-out should cost before opening a business system is in the right place here.

Does this calculator price disposal and the dump trip?

Yes, and separately, because they scale differently. Disposal is entered per gallon, so it rises with the tank you actually pumped rather than with the stop. The dump trip is entered as its own fee, because the drive to the treatment plant costs roughly the same whether the truck is carrying one tank or three — which is exactly why a second tank on the same site is usually more profitable than a second stop across town, and why the calculator lets you add extra tanks to one job rather than pricing each as a fresh call. Both feed the same walk-away price as the labour, so a stop that clears its labour and loses money at the plant shows up before you quote it.
